narrative:
Your application was denied because the assessment estimated a 64% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is an elevated risk, and the school used it as the basis for rejecting your admission rather than waiting to see how you perform.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing, recorded in the first decile; in this assessment it pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second strongest factor was your LSAT score of 20, well below the accepted-student average of about 37, and it also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, below the accepted average of about 3.23, was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction: it pushed toward passing and slightly reduced the estimated risk. It was not enough to overcome the two stronger risk signals. Your gender and race were not used in this assessment.

To improve a future application, focus first on the LSAT: a higher score would address the second-largest risk factor. You should also seek advice on strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a structured bar-readiness plan, and ask admissions counselors at target schools how they evaluate applicants with your profile. Consider applying to programs that offer strong academic support and bar preparation, and provide any context that explains your earlier academic performance.
